                                      Outer-Pedal Area Products
                                         in Elliptic Billiards
                                                   Alper Ferudun∗

                                           1 October 2026 (version 1.1)



                                                       Abstract
              For a ﬁxed confocal elliptic-caustic billiard family with least period congruent to two modulo
          four, we prove that the signed area of the outer tangent polygon times the signed area of its pedal
          polygon with respect to any ﬁxed point is constant. Coprime star trajectories are included. The
          tangent-intersection polygon is an explicit aﬃne image of a half-step shift of the billiard orbit.
          After complexiﬁcation, its area and the outer-pedal area have disjoint possible simple-pole sets.
          Central pairing separates the pedal map into two area traces; two reversal symmetries provide the
          complementary zeros that make their product entire and elliptic. This proves invariant k303,a under
          an explicit least-period convention. For the center pedal, the same argument also covers every odd
          period, proving k303,b for all traversal lengths not divisible by four, including repeated traversals.
          We evaluate the six-periodic constant and give exact counterexamples to the unrestricted arbitrary-
          point repeated-list interpretation and to adding period four in the centered case. No absolute
          priority claim is made.


1        Statement and prior context
Let a > b > 0 and 0 < λ < b2 . Fix the confocal ellipses

                                       x2 y 2                     x2     y2
                                 E:       + 2 = 1,         C:         +       = 1.                                 (1)
                                       a2  b                    a2 − λ b2 − λ
Let P = (Pi )i∈Z/N Z be a billiard orbit on E whose sides are tangent to C. Unless explicitly stated
otherwise, N ≥ 3 denotes its least positive period. Every admitted coprime winding number is allowed,
including self-intersecting star trajectories. For a cyclic vector sequence X write
                                                       1∑
                                            A(X) =         det(Xi , Xi+1 ).
                                                       2 i

All areas in this paper are signed shoelace areas, not sums of the absolute areas of bounded faces.
    Let Vi be the intersection of the tangents to E at Pi and Pi+1 . For a ﬁxed point M ∈ R2 , let
Qi (M ) be its perpendicular foot on the tangent to E at Pi . These are the sidelines of the outer tangent
polygon V , not the original billiard chords. Put

                                         A0 = A(V ),        BM = A(Q(M )).

Theorem 1. If N ≡ 2 (mod 4), then for every ﬁxed M ∈ R2 the product A0 BM is constant as the
initial vertex varies through the ﬁxed-caustic family (1).
    ∗
        Mercury Software GmbH. Email: alper@mercurycodelab.com. GitHub: AlperTheKing.


                                                            1
     This is the outer-pedal area-product assertion k303,a of Reznik, Garcia and Koiller [1, 2, Table 4
and §3.4], under the stated least-period convention. Their table does not explicitly deﬁne minimal
period; we make the qualiﬁcation explicit rather than attribute it verbatim to the source. Section 8
shows that repeating a three-periodic trajectory to obtain six entries does not satisfy the unrestricted
list-length version of the assertion. Hyperbolic and degenerate caustics are excluded.

Theorem 2. For M = O, the product A0 BO is constant whenever the closed traversal has length L
not divisible by four. Here L need not be the least period: repeated traversals and all admitted star
windings are included.

    Theorem 2 proves the adjacent centered assertion k303,b in the same source table, without an
additional least-period qualiﬁcation. Its proof is given in Section 6. The period-four obstruction
there explains why the period restriction cannot simply be omitted. This extension is integrated into
the present paper because it uses the same outer polygon and complementary-pole argument, not a
separate discovery of the overlapping even-period case.
    Chávez-Caliz [6, Theorem 6] proves a related product involving the original and outer tangent-
polygon areas for even Poncelet periods. That theorem supplies a closely related complex pole-
cancellation strategy, but its second polygon is not the outer-pedal polygon. Bialy and Tabachnikov
[7, Theorem 4.1] study precisely the feet on boundary tangents for arbitrary ﬁxed points, proving
centroid and squared-distance invariants; those conclusions are diﬀerent from the cyclic signed-area
product here. We use the canonical billiard parametrization of Stachel [3, Theorem 2, pp. 11–12 of the
preprint], and prove the additional tangent-intersection identity and pedal-area cancellations needed
for Theorem 1.

The physical point period is 4K, not 2K. We work on the common elliptic period lattice 4KZ + 4iK 0 Z.
After complexiﬁcation all dot products are bilinear, not Hermitian. The standard identity dn(u+2K) =

For a real nondegenerate billiard chord the two tangents are distinct; the displayed point is their actual
intersection. The formula supplies its meromorphic continuation through any removable complex
exceptions. Since Vi = V (u + ∆ + ih), the determinant of the ﬁxed diagonal linear map in (5) is e0 /c20 ,
which proves (6). In particular the half-step shift cannot be omitted.


3    The pedal map and central pairing
In this and the next two sections we prove Theorem 1 and assume N ≡ 2 (mod 4).
    Direct perpendicular projection onto the tangent in (4) gives

                                              (1 − M · n(u))n(u)
                            QM (u) = M +                         ,
                                                  n(u) · n(u)
                                                                                                        (7)
                                                                                W (u)
                              W (u) = α − d sn2 u,            n(u) · n(u) =           .
                                                                                 αβ
Introduce the meromorphic vector functions

                                       n(u)                          (M · n(u))n(u)
                          U (u) =               ,        RM (u) =                   .
                                    n(u) · n(u)                        n(u) · n(u)

Thus QM − M = U − RM . Translation does not change cyclic signed area: its extra determinant terms
telescope. As N is even and τ is odd, (2) gives

         P (u + (N/2)h) = −P (u),      U (u + (N/2)h) = −U (u),             RM (u + (N/2)h) = RM (u).

Therefore the mixed determinants in A(U − RM ) cancel in opposite pairs, and

                            BM (u) = A((U (u + ih))i ) + A((RM (u + ih))i ).                            (8)

The two negative signs in the quadratic RM term cancel. Identity (8) does not assume that the pedal
polygon itself is centrally symmetric for M 6= 0.




                                                         3
4    All possible complex poles
The common Jacobi pole positions are

                               zp = 2mK + (2n + 1)iK 0 ,          m, n ∈ Z.

They are simple. At the representative zp = iK 0 , the standard shift formulas are

                                             1                               i dn w
                         sn(iK 0 + w) =          ,        cn(iK 0 + w) = −          .               (9)
                                          k sn w                             k sn w
Both are odd in w. Real and imaginary half-period translations only change coordinate signs, so P
and n are odd about every zp . Put Z = zp + K. At the base representative Z = K + iK 0 ,

                                           dn w                             ik 0
                           sn(Z + w) =           ,        cn(Z + w) = −          .                 (10)
                                          k cn w                          k cn w
Hence P and n are even about every translated Z. These are meromorphic identities, not just identities
on the real parameter line; see [4, 5].
     At a Jacobi pole the leading coeﬃcients of sn and cn are nonzero and have ratio cn / sn = ±i. Thus
n · n has a nonzero double-pole coeﬃcient proportional to 1/α − 1/β. It follows that U is holomorphic
there with a zero and RM is holomorphic there. Consequently QM has no pole at a Jacobi pole.

Lemma 4. The possible poles of A0 and BM are, respectively,

                             zp − ∆ − jh     and     Z − ∆ − jh,       j ∈ Z.                      (11)

For N ≡ 2 (mod 4) these sets are disjoint, and every possible pole of either area function is at most
simple.

Proof. The only remaining possible poles of QM are zeros of W . They are exactly

                                Z − ∆, Z + ∆         (mod 2KZ + 2iK 0 Z).                          (12)

Indeed the quarter-period formula and (3) give

                                                      cn2 ∆   α−λ
                                     sn2 (K ± ∆) =      2   =     ;
                                                      dn ∆     α
the imaginary shift then gives sn2 (Z ± ∆) = α/d. The two roots are distinct since 0 < ∆ < K, and
exhaustive because sn2 has order two on the indicated smaller lattice. At either root,
                                    α               β                         λ
                          sn2 u =     ,    cn2 u = − ,          dn2 u = −        .
                                    d               d                        α−λ
All are nonzero. Thus W 0 = −2d sn u cn u dn u 6= 0, and the foot map has at most simple poles at
these roots.
    Formula (6) gives the ﬁrst pole set in (11). A determinant in A cannot have both adjacent vertices
at Jacobi poles unless h ∈ 2KZ. That would require N | 2τ , impossible for a genuine period N ≥ 6.
Hence A0 has at most simple poles. Several nonadjacent vertices can have coincident simple poles, but
adding their contributions cannot increase the order.
    Taking the cyclic trace of (12) gives the second set in (11); the two signs diﬀer by h = 2∆. A
collision of the two area pole sets would require

                          K ∈ hZ + 2KZ,       equivalently 4τ j = N (2ℓ + 1)

                                                      4
for some integers j, ℓ. The left side is divisible by four, whereas the right side is two modulo four.
Thus the sets are disjoint on the full complex lattice.
    It remains to bound the order of BM . At the adjacent pair Z − ∆, Z + ∆, evenness in (10)
gives n(Z − ∆) = n(Z + ∆). The residues of the two feet are parallel to this common normal, so
the double-pole coeﬃcient of their determinant is zero. Translated pairs satisfy the same statement,
possibly with opposite normal signs. The only additional adjacent coincidence could require 4∆ ≡ 0
(mod 2K). In 0 < ∆ < K this means ∆ = K/2, so τ /N = 1/4, incompatible with the primitive period
under consideration. These are all possible adjacent coincidences. Each determinant in the pedal area
therefore has at most a simple pole, as does their sum.


5    Complementary zeros and the proof of the theorem
Both area traces are h-periodic by cyclic reindexing. First consider a possible outer-area pole u =
zp − ∆. Every foot is holomorphic there by Lemma 4. Its normal is
                                                (              )
                                         nj = n zp + (j − 12 )h .

Oddness about zp and the period N h = 4τ K give

                        n1−j = −nj ,      U1−j = −Uj ,       (RM )1−j = (RM )j .

The permutation j 7→ 1 − j reverses cyclic order. Reversal changes the sign of signed area, while
multiplying every vector by −1 does not. Thus

                          A(U ) = −A(U ) = 0,        A(RM ) = −A(RM ) = 0.

By (8), BM (zp − ∆) = 0. This holomorphic zero removes the possible simple pole of A0 in the product.
   Next consider a possible pedal-area pole u = Z − ∆. Equation (6) gives
                                                        e0
                                         A0 (Z − ∆) =       A(Z).
                                                        c20

All the vertices P (Z + jh) are ﬁnite: a Jacobi pole among them would require the excluded relation
K ∈ hZ + 2KZ. By evenness about Z,

                                        P (Z − jh) = P (Z + jh).

The permutation j 7→ −j reverses this polygon without changing its vertices. Therefore A(Z) =
−A(Z) = 0. This is a holomorphic zero of A0 , cancelling the possible simple pole of BM in the
product.
    These arguments apply at every translated pole. Half-period translations only multiply vector
coordinates by signs and preserve the respective oddness, evenness, parallel-residue, and reversal
identities. We have therefore exhausted and removed every possible pole of A0 BM . The product is an
entire function with periods 4K and 4iK 0 . It is bounded on a fundamental parallelogram, so Liouville’s
theorem makes it constant. Restricting to real phases proves Theorem 1.                                  □
    All real tangent intersections are ﬁnite because c0 > 0; all real feet are ﬁnite because n · n > 0. No
division by a polygon area has been used, so a zero signed pedal area is not an exception. Orientation
reversal changes both area signs and leaves the product unchanged.




                                                    5
6    The center pedal and all periods not divisible by four
We now prove Theorem 2. First suppose N is the least period and 4 ∤ N . For M = O we have RM = 0,
so
                                   BO (u) = A((U (u + jh))j )
directly, without using central pairing. This is the crucial change that allows odd periods. The
parametrization, tangent-intersection formula and pole descriptions above do not otherwise need N
even.
    The possible pole sets are still those of (11). At Jacobi poles U is regular with value zero. The
roots of W are still simple and exactly those of (12). Adjacent original vertices could both be at
Jacobi poles only if N | 2τ , impossible for primitive N ≥ 3; hence A0 has at most simple poles. For
BO , evenness of the normal at Z ± ∆ makes the two residues parallel. The possible extra adjacent
coincidence ∆ = K/2 would force primitive N = 4, which is excluded. Thus its poles are also at most
simple.
    Disjointness of the two pole sets again reduces to

                                                4τ j = N (2ℓ + 1).

For odd N the right side is odd; for N ≡ 2 (mod 4) it is two modulo four. Both contradict the left
side. Thus every step in the pole-order and ﬁniteness argument is valid in both claimed period classes,
including all coprime winding numbers.
     At u = zp − ∆, oddness of U about zp and N h = 4τ K give U1−j = −Uj . Reversal and global
negation therefore imply BO = −BO = 0. For odd N , the self-paired index has argument zp + N h/2 =
zp + 2τ K, a removable Jacobi-pole value of U equal to zero. No exceptional undeﬁned vertex is being
ignored. At u = Z −∆, all P (Z +jh) are ﬁnite, and their evenness under j 7→ −j again gives A(Z) = 0
and then A0 (u) = 0. All possible simple poles of A0 BO are removed. The same entire elliptic-function
argument proves constancy for primitive 4 ∤ N .
     Finally let L be any closed traversal length not divisible by four, and let N be its least period.
Since N | L, necessarily 4 ∤ N . For r = L/N , the ordered original, outer and foot polygons are each
repeated r times. Their signed determinant areas are multiplied by r, so the product is multiplied by
r2 . The primitive result proves constancy for this repeated traversal as well. This completes the proof
of Theorem 2.                                                                                         □

Proposition 5. The centered product is not constant on every four-periodic family. For any a > b > 0
and λ = a2 b2 /(a2 + b2 ), two members of the same family have products 8a2 b2 and 2(a2 + b2 )2 , diﬀering
by 2(a2 − b2 )2 > 0.

Proof. The axis diamond (a, 0), (0, b), (−a, 0), (0, −b) is a billiard trajectory; its slanted sidelines satisfy
(a2 −λ)/a2 +(b2 −λ)/b2 = 1, the confocal tangency equation. The outer tangent polygon is the rectangle
with vertices (±a, ±b), of area 4ab. Its center feet are the original diamond vertices, of area 2ab.
    Put s = a2 + b2 . The second trajectory is the axis-parallel rectangle with cyclic vertices

                              (a2 , b2 )   (−a2 , b2 )     (−a2 , −b2 )
                                                                 (a2 , −b2 )
                                √ ,          √         ,      √     √   ,    .
                                   s           s                 s     s
                                                                     √
Its vertices lie on E, and its normals have coordinate magnitudes 1/ s, so the horizontal and vertical
sides obey the reﬂection law. The identities a2 − λ = a4 /s and b2 − λ = b4 /s show that its sides
                                                                                       √
are tangent to the same caustic. Its boundary tangent lines have equations ±x ± y = s, giving an
                                                              √         √
outer diamond of area 2s. Their center feet are the corners (± s/2, ± s/2), of area s. The two area
products and their stated diﬀerence follow.


                                                           6
    For a = 5, b = 3, these products are 1800 and 2312, with the same λ = 225/34. This refutes
an all-period extension, not Theorem 2. Exact checks also give product 243/64 in ﬁve three-periodic
instances with a2 = 1, b2 = 3/8, λ = 9/25, and verify the r2 scaling on repeated lengths 6, 9, 15. These
checks supplement the analytic proof; they do not establish general constancy by sampling. No exact
ﬁve-periodic control is claimed.


7    Dependence on the pedal point and the six-periodic constant
There is a useful algebraic description of the arbitrary-point dependence. For any cyclic collection of
lines ni · X = 1 with nonzero real normals, put si = ni · ni and Di = det(ni , ni+1 ). Translating the
foot polygon by −M gives the exact identity

                                            1 ∑ Di (1 − ni · M )(1 − ni+1 · M )
                                BM =                                            .                             (13)
                                            2 i              si si+1

For n = (x, y), q = (z, w), D = xw − yz, s = x2 + y 2 , t = z 2 + w2 ,

                        D(xz − yw) = szw − txy,                 D(xw + yz) = sw2 − ty 2 .

After division by st, both expressions telescope when summed cyclically. Thus the homogeneous
quadratic part of (13) is radial. For even primitive N , central pairing eliminates the linear part,
yielding
                                           1 ∑ Di (ni · ni+1 )   1∑ (                 )
              BM = B0 + C|M |2 ,     C=                        =     sin 2(ϕi+1 − ϕi ) ,        (14)
                                           4 i     si si+1       8 i

where ϕi is a real normal angle. It follows that the invariant in Theorem 1 has the form C0 + C2 |M |2
for the ﬁxed conic pair.

Proposition 6. For the six-periodic family with λ = a2 b2 /(a + b)2 ,
                                                                  (                  )
                                 0                              |M |2
                                A BM = ab(a + 2b)(2a + b) 1 +                            .                    (15)
                                                              (a + b)2
                                                                               √
Proof. By Theorem 1, it suﬃces to evaluate one member. Put r =                     b(2a + b) and s = a + b. Take

                 P1 = (a, 0),    P2 = (a2 /s, br/s),        P3 = (−a2 /s, br/s),             Pi+3 = −Pi .

Since a2 + r2 = s2 , all six distinct vertices lie on E. At P1 the horizontal normal reﬂects direction
(a, r) to (−a, r). At P2 the normal (1/s, r/(bs)) has squared length 2/(bs) and dot product 1 with
(−a, r), so reﬂection sends that direction to (−s, 0). Symmetry veriﬁes the other reﬂections. The
horizontal edge is tangent to the caustic because b2 − λ = b2 r2 /s2 ; the slant-edge tangency identity
is λ(r2 + a2 ) = a2 b2 . Its contact parameter from P1 to P2 is b/s ∈ (0, 1), so the contacts lie on the
segments. Thus this is a genuine six-periodic member.
     Its outer vertices and center feet are, respectively,

                          V1 = (a, b2 /r), V2 = (0, bs/r),  V3 = (−a, b2 /r),
                          Q1 = (a, 0),     Q2 = (b/2, r/2), Q3 = (−b/2, r/2),

with Vi+3 = −Vi and Qi+3 = −Qi . Shoelace evaluation gives

                                            2ab(a + 2b)                r(2a + b)
                                     A0 =               ,       B0 =             .
                                                 r                         2

                                                            7
Writing ϕ = arg(b+ir), the normal-angle increments are ϕ, π−2ϕ, ϕ, repeated twice. Since sin 2ϕ = r/s
and sin2 ϕ = (2a + b)/(2s),

                                    4 sin 2ϕ − 2 sin 4ϕ   r(2a + b)  B0
                              C=                        =           = 2.
                                             8               2s2      s
Substitution in (14) proves (15).

    For example, a = 5, b = 3 gives λ = 225/64 and A0 BM = 2145(1 + |M |2 /64). The supplementary
standard-library checker independently reconstructs six-periodic orbits for four semiaxis pairs and four
initial phases, veriﬁes their reﬂection laws and strict caustic contacts, and checks all coeﬃcients of the
quadratic area polynomial. The circle case among those controls is not needed for the theorem’s a > b
domain. These sixteen orbit instances are ﬁnite checks, not the proof of all-family invariance.


8    Least period, reproducibility and limitations
The least-period qualiﬁcation in Theorem 1, for arbitrary M , cannot be dropped in favor of arbitrary
list length. The centered Theorem 2 has the separate repetition argument already proved above. Fix
                                                 3          9
                               a2 = 1,       b2 = ,   λ=       ,   M = (1, 0).
                                                 8          25
The triangle                        (          ( √ ) (     √ ))
                                              4 3 6    4 3 6
                              P =    (1, 0), − ,    , − ,−
                                              5 20     5   20
and its central reﬂection −P are genuine three-periodic billiards with this same caustic. At P , the in-
coming and outgoing directions √  at (1, 0) reﬂect in the horizontal normal. At the upper-left vertex
                                                                                                    √their
representative directions (−12, 6) and (0, −1) satisfy the reﬂection law with normal (−4/5, 2 6/5);
the remaining vertex follows by symmetry. The vertical side is tangent because a2 − λ = 16/25, and
the two slant sides satisfy the confocal tangency equation. These identities and strict segment contacts
are also checked exactly in the supplement.
    For P the outer area and pedal area at M are
                                                √                 √
                                         0   27 6               81 6
                                      A =          ,     BM =         ,
                                               16                200
while for −P they are                      √              √
                                        27 6
                                         0              21 6
                                   A =        ,  BM =        .
                                          16             200
The respective products are 6561/1600 and 1701/1600. Repeating each list twice produces six entries
and doubles both signed areas, giving products
                                             6561              1701
                                                      and           .
                                             400               400
Their diﬀerence is 243/20 > 0. This refutes the padded-list extension, not Theorem 1: these orbits
still have least period three and do not have the even-orbit central pairing used in (8).
     The supplement uses exact rational polynomial arithmetic and real quadratic ﬁelds. It veriﬁes the
two universal telescoping identities behind (14), elementary axis identities, the six-periodic controls,
and the padded triangle countercontrol. The general theorem rests on the written analytic argument,
not on those ﬁnite checks or on numerical exploration.


                                                       8
    The source conjecture, confocal geometry, Jacobi parametrization and complex pole-cancellation
method are credited prior mathematics. A bounded primary-literature search did not locate an earlier
proof of this precise arbitrary-point outer-pedal product. This is not evidence of absolute priority, and
the source’s historical question mark is not itself a statement about the current literature. The closest
cited area-product and arbitrary-point projection results concern diﬀerent quantities, as described in
Section 1.
    This is an unrefereed preprint. AI assistance was used in derivation, internal checking, coding and
manuscript preparation. No independent human peer review or formal proof-assistant veriﬁcation is
claimed.
